title: The Capital Order Problem: Why the Most Expensive Money Gets Raised First
linkedin:
Most growing businesses treat capital as one pool: money is money, find enough of it.

But every dollar of funding has a different price tag, and the order you raise it in matters almost as much as the amount.

Retained profit is the cheapest capital you'll ever use. Asset or debtor finance comes next, priced against something tangible. Bank term debt sits above that, priced against the whole balance sheet. Mezzanine costs more again.

Equity is the most expensive money a business can raise. Not because the cheque is large, but because it never ends. It's not a cost for this year, it's a permanent share of every year of profit from the day the raise completes.

And yet we see it reached for first more often than last. Usually not out of carelessness. A bank says no on serviceability before cheaper, asset-specific options get explored. An investor conversation already underway feels easier than the slower work of structuring debt properly. Growth arrives with a deadline attached, and the fastest yes wins.

The businesses that fund growth well work through the same sequence every time: retained profit first, then finance tied to the specific asset or receivable, then bank debt sized against serviceability, then mezzanine for the gap. Equity is the last call, only for what genuinely can't be funded any other way.

Getting the order right rarely changes how much you raise. It changes how much of the business, and how much of next year's profit, is still yours once the money has done its job.

Quick question for the business owners here: when you've needed money to fund growth, what did you reach for first? Your own cash, a loan, or an investor?

We see a lot of businesses go to equity early and leave cheaper options on the table. Fair enough, it feels simpler than wrangling a bank. But equity is the one form of capital that never stops costing you. It's a permanent slice of every future year of profit, not just this year's.

The order you raise money in matters almost as much as how much you raise. Worth thirty minutes with a coffee and a calculator before the next big decision lands.

A note for business owners across Brisbane, Queensland and the East Coast as spring growth decisions, a new hire, a new site, a piece of equipment, start landing on the desk.

When it's time to fund that growth, most owners treat the money as one pool. Find enough of it, wherever it comes from. In practice, every source of capital has a different cost, and the order you approach them in matters.

Retained profit is the cheapest money you'll use. Finance tied to a specific asset or to outstanding invoices comes next. Bank term debt sits above that. Equity is almost always the most expensive, because it isn't a cost that ends when it's repaid. It's a permanent share of every year of profit the business makes from that point on.

What we see most often is that order running backwards under time pressure. A bank says no before cheaper options get a proper look, or an investor conversation already underway feels like the easier path. The fix is working through the cheaper layers first: retained profit, asset finance, bank debt, and only then equity for whatever genuinely can't be funded another way.
